entry.evidence: Considering that timeliness is of the essence in rapid earthquake characterisation, it becomes important to find an optimum duration for the input data

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML text (jats_text) of Chakraborty et al. 2022, checked against the PDF

steps.action: The authors take from the EEW literature the expectation that magnitude estimates become more accurate with longer input data.
steps.quote: The accuracy of such estimates has been shown to increase with the duration of data used to calculate them (Ziv, 2014).

steps.action: The authors pose the question of an optimum input duration for a single-station deep-learning magnitude classifier (noise, low, high magnitude, boundary ML 5.0).
steps.quote: it becomes important to find an optimum duration for the input data

steps.action: The authors try magnitudes 3 and 4 as alternative decision boundaries and report similar accuracy, precision and recall, without giving the numbers.
steps.quote: Magnitudes of 3 and 4 were also experimented with as decision boundaries

steps.action: The authors draw waveforms from the STEAD archive and keep only ML-scale traces with SNR of at least 10 dB.
steps.quote: We also discard traces with signal-to-noise ratio less than 10 dB for quality control.

steps.action: The authors split the data 60:10:30 into non-overlapping training, validation and test sets by event and by noise station, and set five P-wave input durations with 2.8–3.0 s of pre-signal noise.
steps.quote: we investigate the effect of using different lengths of data after the first P arrival (1, 3, 10, 20 and 30 s)

steps.action: The authors rebalance the classes: they augment high-magnitude events with shifted windows and polarity flips, undersample low-magnitude and noise traces, and set a 1:1:10 class weight chosen experimentally.
steps.quote: To tackle this imbalance problem, we apply resampling of the data (Krawczyk, 2016) as follows.

steps.action: The authors adopt the CNN plus bi-LSTM softmax architecture from their own earlier conference abstract.
steps.quote: The model architecture (Chakraborty et al., 2021) consists of two sets of 1D convolution

steps.action: The authors train one model per input duration with Adam, categorical cross-entropy, batch size 256, early stopping and a learning-rate schedule, keeping the epoch with the lowest validation loss.
steps.quote: Early stopping (Prechelt, 2012) is used to prevent overfitting

steps.action: The authors define accuracy, precision and recall, show correctly classified examples, and show softmax probabilities for one magnitude-2.8 waveform at all five lengths.
steps.quote: the predicted probabilities are different and show no dependence on the length of input data

steps.action: The authors compare test-set accuracy, precision and recall across the five input durations.
steps.quote: Figure 6a shows the variation in the model performance with respect to the duration of P-wave data used as an input.

steps.action: The authors retrain the 3 s model five times on the same data with untuned random seeds and judge the variation across durations comparable to the retraining spread.
steps.quote: we also looked at the randomness in the performance when the model is trained on the same data five times

steps.action: The authors examine the confusion matrix and per-magnitude misclassification of one 3 s model, finding errors concentrated near ML 5.0 and biased toward false high-magnitude alarms by the class weights.
steps.quote: the misclassification of low-magnitude events as high-magnitude and vice versa is most pronounced at the decision boundary of 5.0

steps.action: The authors break down classification results by hypocentral distance and SNR, finding correct classifications across wide ranges and noise misclassifications clustered below 20 dB.
steps.quote: there are instances of correct classification across a wide-range of hypocentral distances and signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs)

steps.action: The authors attribute residual errors within 5.0 ± 0.5 to uncertainty in catalogue magnitude labels rather than to the model.
steps.quote: even magnitudes of the same scale reported by different agencies can vary by as much as 0.5 magnitude units

steps.action: The authors propose recasting the task as regression in a future version; this is not performed here.
steps.quote: it might be helpful to treat this as a regression problem instead of classification

steps.action: The authors set the overall accuracy of 90.04–93.86 % against the 93.67 % reported by Saad et al. (2020) with three stations.
steps.quote: comparable to the magnitude classification accuracy of 93.67 % achieved by Saad et al. (2020)

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that input length from 1 to 30 s has no significant effect on classifier performance, with accuracy up to 93.86 %.
steps.quote: changing the length of the waveform (1, 3, 10, 20 or 30 s after P arrival) has no significant effect on the model performance

tree.answer: Dependence of a deep-learning magnitude classifier's performance on P-wave input length
Yes; performance measured directly on a labelled held-out test set
Characterize a single-station classifier and find a minimum adequate input duration
No rivals stated; only an implicit cited expectation that longer data improve estimates
Not derived; no rival's prediction computed
Set computationally: five input durations, one model trained per duration
Partly; the duration effect is within the retraining spread (3 s only); boundary change and distance/SNR breakdown are qualitative
Input length has no significant effect; accuracy 90.04–93.86 %
Not assessable; no review file or discussion supplied

end.claim: A single-station CNN–bi-LSTM classifier separates noise, low-magnitude and high-magnitude (ML ≥ 5.0) waveforms with accuracy up to 93.86 %, and changing the input length from 1 to 30 s after P arrival has no significant effect on its performance.

decisive_move.sentence: Retraining the 3 s model five times on the same data gave the spread against which the variation across durations was judged insignificant; without it the no-effect claim has no reference.

gates.evidence: Action: the question of optimum duration directed the design of five input lengths (§2.1 ¶2), but no hypothesis was stated as the authors' own; the longer-is-better expectation is only cited (§1 ¶1). Claim: the no-effect claim could have failed if the variation across durations had exceeded the retraining spread (§4 ¶1). The judgement is visual ('comparable'), uses five retrains at 3 s only, and applies no statistical test. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data. The class weight was 'chosen experimentally' and the boundary is 'arbitrarily chosen' (§1 ¶3, §2.1 ¶3).

imports.item: 1D convolutional neural networks, bi-directional LSTM layers, dropout, max-pooling, softmax output
Adam optimiser, categorical cross-entropy, early stopping, learning-rate reduction
Class-imbalance handling by resampling and class weights; data augmentation techniques from image processing
Accuracy, precision, recall and confusion matrix as evaluation metrics
Random-seed effects on model stability (Bengio 2012; Madhyastha and Jain 2019)

limits: No review file, open discussion, or earlier version was supplied, although the paper went through Solid Earth discussion from 30 May 2022, so no review sequence is coded. The decision-boundary test with magnitudes 3 and 4 (§1 ¶3) is reported in a single sentence with no numbers. The retraining spread (Fig. 6b) is measured only for the 3 s duration, and the 'no significant effect' judgement is visual, with no statistical test. Inference: five retrains may understate the seed variance. The held-out test set comes from the same STEAD archive and split, so there is no independent dataset or region. The comparison with Saad et al. (2020) uses different data and stations, so it is a loose baseline, not a controlled comparison. The architecture is inherited from the authors' own EGU abstract (Chakraborty et al., 2021), and how it was chosen is not reported. Sub-claims and their statuses: (a) accuracy of 90.04–93.86 % across durations: capability_characterized. (b) The model classifies across wide ranges of hypocentral distance and SNR and does not directly correlate amplitude or SNR with magnitude (§4 ¶3): capability_characterized, qualitative only, read off a scatter plot. (c) The decision boundary does not influence performance (§1 ¶3): asserted without data shown. (d) Over-classification of ML 4.5–5.0 events as high-magnitude is caused by the class weights (§4 ¶2): attributed, not tested by varying the weights. Composition is none_fits because the walk is an engineering characterization of a method with one varied parameter and no stated rival. The question precedes the capability, so capability_first does not fit, and no phenomenon is stabilised before a question, so exploration_first does not fit. The paper makes no explicit 'first' or 'previously unknown' statement.

disagreements.target: Traditional EEW magnitude methods in which estimate accuracy increases with the duration of input data (Ziv, 2014)
disagreements.support: Models trained on 1, 3, 10, 20 and 30 s of P-wave data vary no more than five retrains of the 3 s model on the same data.
disagreements.quote: In traditional EEW methods, the robustness in the estimation of earthquake parameters has been observed to increase with the length of input data.

disagreements.target: Saad et al. (2020), three-station deep-learning classification of earthquake parameters
disagreements.support: A single-station model reaches 90.04–93.86 % accuracy against their 93.67 %, implying three stations are not required for comparable accuracy (different data, not a controlled comparison).
disagreements.quote: comparable to the magnitude classification accuracy of 93.67 % achieved by Saad et al. (2020) using data from three seismic stations

alternatives_considered.reason: Arbitrarily chosen; can be modified with the model's purpose and local geology

alternatives_considered.chosen: Only traces with magnitude given in the ML (local magnitude) scale
alternatives_considered.reason: To ensure consistency in magnitude; ML is the case for most traces

alternatives_considered.chosen: Class weight 1:1:10 for noise, low and high magnitude
alternatives_considered.reason: High-magnitude class still under-represented after resampling

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Normalising the data, as in Lomax et al. (2019)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Data used without instrument response removal

alternatives_considered.reason: A single type would significantly reduce training data, limiting the learning

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Treating magnitude as a regression problem (future version)
alternatives_considered.reason: Regression would give the model more information about the exact magnitude
